Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

vignette: John is a 25-year-old European male who works as a salesperson in a bustling city. He grew up in a peaceful small town but moved to the city for better job opportunities after his parents passed away when he was young. John has always been someone who takes pride in his work and enjoys a good social life with friends and family. However, his life took a drastic turn two years ago when he found himself trapped in a war zone during a business trip. The traumatic event occurred unexpectedly on a routine sales visit to a client's office in a volatile region of the Middle East. John was in his hotel room when explosions began to rock the city around him. Terrified and confused, he watched helplessly as buildings crumbled and sirens wailed outside. He could hear screams and gunfire from the streets below, and the sight of people running for cover while shrapnel rained down made an indelible mark on his psyche. Since that day, John has been struggling with intense negative emotions such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. The memories of those moments are vivid and intrusive, often replaying in his mind unbidden. He finds himself startled by sudden loud noises or the sight of uniformed individuals, reminders of the chaos he witnessed during the explosions. The night has become a particularly fraught time for John. He finds it much harder to feel safe at night than during the day. The darkness amplifies his sense of vulnerability, and he often lies awake in bed, scanning his surroundings for any signs of danger. Even with all the lights on and windows locked, he feels exposed and unprotected. Concentration has also become a significant challenge for John. Simple tasks that once came easily to him now require immense effort and focus. At work, he finds it difficult to keep up with meetings and client interactions without his mind wandering back to the traumatic event. This struggle has affected his performance at work; deadlines are missed, and mistakes have started to pile up, leading to tensions with his manager. John's relationship with his girlfriend has also been strained by these changes in him. He finds it hard to engage in conversations that don't revolve around work or pastimes that he used to enjoy together. What frightens him most is the fear of burdening her with his constant anxiety and the worry that she might leave him because he can no longer be the partner she needs. John's avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his daily life as well. He avoids certain areas in the city, particularly those with heavy pedestrian traffic or large crowds, which remind him of the chaos he experienced during the war zone incident. This has led to him taking long detours to avoid these places, causing him to be late for work and meetings more frequently. What finally brought John to seek help was a combination of mounting stress at work and growing concerns about his deteriorating relationship with his girlfriend. He had come to believe that he could not continue living this way; the constant vigilance and emotional turmoil were taking their toll on every aspect of his life. John is most hoping for relief from his intense negative emotions and a sense of safety, both during the day and at night. He dreams of regaining his ability to concentrate and re-establishing a sense of normalcy in his daily life.
